pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words, answered about the actual project, issue and PR they worked on rather than in the abstract; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Why this project and this issue? Give me the signals you checked, with dates, and the triage answers that made the issue safe to start.
expected_points: health signals with evidence rather than adjectives: commit recency, maintainer reply latency, merged PRs from non-maintainers, unassigned recent good-first-issue labels, a CONTRIBUTING.md that describes the real process, CI on PRs
merged PRs from outsiders is the strongest single signal — labels without outside merges are labels, not a pipeline
triage: reproduced on the current default branch, nobody else already on it, a maintainer wants it, it is in scope, and the size estimate includes test, docs and review rounds
prefers a project they use and a subsystem they can read, over prestige or star count
names the weakest signal on the chosen project and what they would do if it bit them

questions.prompt: Explain how the subsystem you patched works, as if I maintain it. How did you find the code path, and what could your change break?
expected_points: describes the code as it was before the change, not just the diff
names the technique that actually worked: grepping the exact error or output string, starting from a failing test, following one call chain, reading types before functions
got the project building and its suite green before editing anything, so later red is theirs
used git log or blame to learn why the code is the way it is
names concrete blast radius: callers, platforms, exported API, downstream behaviour

questions.prompt: What did CONTRIBUTING.md require, and where did following their conventions mean doing something differently from how you would do it in your own capstone?
expected_points: how to run tests as CI does, style and lint requirements, commit and PR conventions, DCO sign-off or CLA — and that the legal step is done early because it blocks a merge indefinitely
matched local test style, error vocabulary, naming and comment style rather than personal preference
gofmt clean and vet clean before pushing
no new dependency without asking, and no new exported API sneaked in
a specific example of a preference they suppressed because it was not their codebase

questions.prompt: Walk me through your PR: why is the diff that size, what did you leave out, and what does the description tell a reviewer who has forgotten the issue?
expected_points: one concern per PR; a second bug becomes a second issue, not more diff
no drive-by refactors or reformatting — they add review surface and wreck git blame
a regression test that fails before and passes after, stated as a claim the reviewer can check
description carries what changed, why this approach and what was rejected, how it was tested, and what was deliberately left out
smaller PRs get reviewed sooner; making the maintainer's yes cheap is the actual leverage

questions.prompt: Take the review comment you liked least. What did you do with it — and where does disagreeing stop?
expected_points: three legitimate responses: agree and fix, ask a narrow question with a proposal, or disagree once with evidence
assumes the maintainer has context not visible in the code — a downstream consumer, an old bug, a platform difference
replies on every thread rather than silently pushing, and re-requests review once when done
implementing something they disagree with is a normal outcome, stated plainly and moved past
repeating an argument after a decision, or taking it to another channel, is how a mergeable PR dies

questions.prompt: What was different about working in someone else's codebase, and what will you do differently on the next contribution?
expected_points: concrete differences: settled conventions, invisible history, no authority to change the design, a reviewer who owes them nothing
something the maintainer knew that could not be read off the code
a specific misjudgement — diff size, a claim posted before reproducing, an assumption about the subsystem that was wrong
three specific changes for next time rather than general resolutions
what it changed about their own project's front door: README, contribution docs, tests a stranger can run

questions.prompt: What makes a claim comment worth replying to, and what do you do during three weeks of silence?
expected_points: a claim shows evidence of reproduction, the code path found, a proposed approach small enough to argue with, one or two narrow questions, and a rough timeline
read CONTRIBUTING first and follow it over any general advice; claim one issue at a time and say so publicly if you drop it
silence is the default state of open source; one polite ping after two full weeks, and no more
keep the branch rebased and CI-green; spend the wait on a second small issue, a review of someone else's PR, or docs
on a small clearly-scoped bug, sending the patch after a week of silence is reasonable; on anything larger, silence means do not build it yet

questions.prompt: Your PR gets closed. What are the likely reasons, what do you say, and why is that not a failed lesson?
expected_points: scope, project direction, maintenance burden, timing, or someone got there first — usually not code quality
reply once, thank them, and ask what would have made it acceptable; that answer is the most valuable output
do not argue, reopen, or repost elsewhere
the merge was never theirs to control — the process and the review conversation are what is graded
an unrequested feature is the most commonly rejected contribution, which is why maintainer agreement comes before code
